routes.description: Establish that Christian belief can remain rational when treated as an evidence-sensitive cumulative worldview whose historical, textual, philosophical, and moral components are assessed together rather than as isolated claims requiring certainty.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if it supplies a coherent evidential account of faith, a cumulative basis for the resurrection and Christian distinctiveness, a qualified model of scriptural reliability, and morally relevant explanations of hiddenness, judgment, and sincere nonbelief.

motionBridge.description: Show that the combined Christian account has sufficient evidential and explanatory support to remain rationally sustainable amid the specified skeptical challenges.

centralBridges.description: Define faith as evidence-grounded trust under uncertainty and explain why contrary possibilities do not by themselves make that trust irrational.
Provide a cumulative historical case for resurrection that compares testimony, textual reliability, relevant historical considerations, and alternative explanations.
Defend a model in which culturally situated, composite, and fallible human transmission can still preserve evidentially and theologically relevant scriptural meaning.
Explain why limited divine disclosure and present religious commitment can serve moral transformation while judgment remains compatible with sincere evidential limitations.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Show how qualified historical claims about the Exodus and Jesus can survive objections based on archaeology, ancient conventions, and literary dependence.
Distinguish Christianity from rival traditions and alleged parallels through case-specific comparison rather than assuming either uniqueness or parity.

routes.description: Establish that withholding Christian belief is rational because the available disclosure, testimony, textual record, historical support, and moral account do not adequately distinguish Christianity from naturalistic explanations or competing traditions.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if ordinary evidential expectations, sincere nonbelief, scriptural development, historical uncertainty, religious diversity, and alternative explanations jointly undercut the warrant claimed for distinctively Christian conclusions.

motionBridge.description: Show that the available evidence does not sufficiently distinguish Christian supernatural claims from error, cultural development, or rival religious claims.

centralBridges.description: Argue that evidence-based belief requires clearer disclosure than sincere nonbelievers presently receive and that biblical models do not resolve this disparity.
Show why ancient resurrection testimony and related historical claims require stronger support before overcoming ordinary experience and alternative explanations.
Explain how textual variation, internal diversity, literary reuse, discrepancies, and culturally situated authorship weaken claims of reliable divine communication.
Press whether hell, postmortem opportunity, and the asserted present necessity of belief coherently address sincere skepticism and limited evidence.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Use population, archaeological, and interpretive difficulties in the Exodus traditions to test their historical and religious evidential force.
Use competing religions, recurring supernatural motifs, and naturalistic accounts of religious experience to challenge Christian epistemic privilege.

sections.title: Evidential Faith, Divine Hiddenness, and Adequate Disclosure
sections.rationale: This issue tests the governing conception of rational faith and whether testimonial or prior evidence can justify trust when sincere nonbelievers lack the clearer disclosure they regard as necessary.

sections.title: Hell, Sincere Nonbelief, and the Present Value of Commitment
sections.rationale: This issue bears on whether Christian belief offers a coherent moral account of judgment, freely chosen separation, postmortem recognition, and the significance of commitment during earthly life.

sections.title: Resurrection Testimony and Cumulative Historical Evidence
sections.rationale: The resurrection is a central distinctively Christian claim, making the adequacy of testimony, burial and empty-tomb considerations, document reliability, ordinary expectations, and rival explanations indispensable.

sections.title: Biblical Reliability, Human Composition, and Literary Development
sections.rationale: This issue determines whether textual variants, discrepancies, composite authorship, apostolic disagreement, and literary reuse are compatible with scripture functioning as reliable evidence and divine communication.

sections.title: Exodus Historicity, Archaeology, and Ancient Conventions
sections.rationale: The dispute over a minimal migration, population figures, conquest traditions, archaeological absence, and ancient numerical conventions provides a focused test of biblical historical reasoning.

sections.title: Religious Pluralism, Ancient Parallels, and Religious Experience
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether Christianity can be non-question-beggingly distinguished from rival scriptures, recurring supernatural traditions, alleged literary parallels, and naturalistic explanations of spiritual experience.

moves.speaker: Derek Lambert
moves.proposition: Condemning a sincere former Christian who remains open to God but finds the available evidence implausible would make hell difficult to reconcile with morally responsible nonbelief.
moves.attributionBasis: Lambert identifies himself as an atheist and former fundamentalist before posing the direct challenge about his own fate.

response.rationale: This constructive move directly raises the moral compatibility of hell with sincere, evidence-sensitive nonbelief and therefore establishes a central challenge.

moves.speaker: Michael Jones

components.text: Whether hell condemns a sincere skeptic merely because earthly time expires.
Whether Lambert's evidential sincerity is compatible with a freely chosen separation from God.

response.rationale: The reply rejects an automatic deadline model and supplies a chosen-identity account of hell, but it does not explain why this sincere skeptic's nonbelief constitutes that choice.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the punishment model decisively but leaves the sincerity-to-voluntary-separation bridge unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The account is clearly stated as Jones's worldview, and death is expressly denied the status of necessarily being the final choice.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Jones presents a qualified account of hell as his view and explicitly avoids claiming that earthly death necessarily ends all opportunity.

charity.alternative: The skeptic's nonbelief may be involuntary rather than a chosen identity opposed to God.
charity.decisiveQualification: The reply must connect sincere evidential nonbelief to voluntary separation, not merely redefine hell.

components.text: If choice remains after death, why present Christian belief is necessary now.
Whether present happiness after leaving Christianity bears on a supposedly freely chosen hell identity.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly identifies and presses the central implication of allowing meaningful recognition and choice after death.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Lambert frames the point as a conditional question and qualifies the autobiographical happiness claim appropriately.

routes.description: Establish that a distinctively Christian account integrates divine encounter, suffering, consciousness, objective morality, moral motivation, and historical moral development more coherently than the agnostic or naturalistic alternatives under discussion.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if Christian claims about incarnation, resurrection, Trinitarian goodness, human dignity, and scripture-guided development jointly address the principal objections while supplying comparative explanatory resources unavailable or less unified on the alternatives.

motionBridge.description: Connect the Christian accounts of hiddenness, evil, consciousness, morality, and moral progress into a unified comparative explanation of the phenomena named in the motion.

centralBridges.description: Explain how conscious participation in reality and personal divine self-disclosure can coexist with experiences of absence, nonbelief, and religious variation.
Show how divine participation in suffering, human epistemic limits, and resurrection hope jointly address apparently gratuitous evil without denying its moral seriousness.
Ground objective goodness and obligation in eternal interpersonal divine love while avoiding both arbitrary command and a standard independent of God.
Provide a prospective, Jesus-centered scriptural criterion and historical mechanism for distinguishing moral development from corruption or regression.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Relate modern equality and human-rights commitments to Christian conceptions of persons and assess whether materialism can sustain the inherited claims.
Explain how Christian narrative and communal practices connect moral truth to motivation and sustain its application under changing conditions.

routes.description: Show that hiddenness and apparently gratuitous suffering remain evidential or internal difficulties for Christian theism, while non-theistic moral resources and a critical account of historical development prevent Christianity from gaining the claimed comparative advantage.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the proposed Christian explanations leave unresolved tensions concerning divine love, inscrutability, moral authority, and retrospective moral interpretation, while agnostic or naturalistic alternatives retain adequate accounts of moral judgment, motivation, convergence, and change.

motionBridge.description: Demonstrate that the combined evidence from hiddenness, evil, morality, and moral history does not establish Christianity as the better overall account relative to the stated alternatives.

centralBridges.description: Establish why geographic contingency, sincere nonbelief, spiritual dryness, and unresolved religious disagreement remain difficult to reconcile with an all-loving relational God.
Preserve the force of apparently gratuitous suffering while testing whether appeals to inscrutable reasons undermine other arguments that depend on intelligible divine purposes.
Test whether divine power, goodness, and Trinitarian love uniquely yield obligation or motivation, and identify non-theistic routes to moral judgment and action.
Require non-retrospective criteria that distinguish authentic Christian development from corruption and explain both discovery of timeless truths and prospective regression.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Assess whether unknown relationship through goodness can mitigate hiddenness only by requiring inclusivist access to salvation beyond explicit Christian belief.
Account for the motivational roles of shared narratives and moral emotion while separating those roles from claims of uniquely Christian truth or derivation.

sections.title: Hiddenness, Consciousness, and Divine Encounter
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether ordinary conscious and rational life, incarnation, resistance, and participation in goodness can account for divine relationship despite non-resistant unbelief, geographic variation, spiritual dryness, and doctrinal disagreement.

sections.title: Evil, Suffering, and Divine Inscrutability
sections.rationale: Apparently gratuitous suffering directly burdens the Christian account, while divine participation, resurrection, internal moral critique, and the broader consequences of appealing to inscrutable purposes define the principal clash.

sections.title: Objective Morality, Obligation, and Motivation
sections.rationale: The comparative case turns substantially on whether Christianity uniquely grounds objective goodness and obligation, avoids the Euthyphro dilemma, and connects moral knowledge to motivation more adequately than realist or anti-realist alternatives.

sections.title: Human Dignity, Narrative, and Moral Progress
sections.rationale: Claims about Christian sources of human rights require examination alongside historical corruption, narrative transmission, scriptural criteria, gradual moral discovery, future applications, regression, and embodied practices of moral formation.

routes.description: Establish that evaluative and moral concepts arise from factual requirements faced by living, choosing human beings, and that those requirements support objective guidance for flourishing and social conduct.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if it identifies life-relevant facts as the referents and standard of evaluation, explains how those facts guide volitional human action, and derives non-arbitrary principles for individual and interpersonal conduct.

motionBridge.description: Connect the factual requirements of human life to truth-apt standards governing choices, actions, and character.

centralBridges.description: Explain why living organisms' conditional requirements create the factual basis and practical need for evaluative concepts.
Show how a human choice to live makes facts about survival and flourishing action-guiding without treating value as an intrinsic property.
Derive rights and constraints on force from human rational agency and each person's need to act on independent judgment.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Distinguish emotions accompanying evaluation from the cognitive identification of life-supporting or life-destructive facts.
Apply the life-based standard consistently across immortality, psychopath, animal-treatment, and consent cases.

routes.description: Establish that moral utterances express non-truth-apt emotional attitudes and that factual descriptions of life, agency, or flourishing do not themselves supply objective oughtness or binding interpersonal duties.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if it provides a coherent emotivist account of moral language and experience while showing that the proposed life standard cannot non-circularly bridge facts to objective norms or explain its disputed applications.

motionBridge.description: Account for moral claims as emotive expressions while denying that life-related facts constitute objective moral properties or truth conditions.

centralBridges.description: Specify what moral predicates express and require the objectivist alternative to identify the alleged objective oughtness.
Show why a pre-moral choice to live or a factual description of flourishing cannot generate objective normative authority.
Test whether actor-centered life and flourishing can justify rights or condemn advantageous harm without assuming the disputed morality.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain how emotive advocacy, rational inference, and useful rights conventions can function without objective moral truth.
Use immortality, atypical agents, and animal treatment to test the scope and consistency of the life-based account.

sections.title: Moral Meaning, Emotion, and Objective Reference
sections.rationale: This issue defines the motion-level disagreement over whether moral predicates report life-relevant facts or express attitudes without truth conditions, and it fixes what either side must explain about moral language and cognition.

sections.title: Life, Choice, and the Foundation of Value
sections.rationale: This issue covers the proposed dependence of value on living action and the choice to remain alive, together with the challenge that a conditional or pre-moral choice cannot establish objective value.

sections.title: From Life Facts to Oughts and Flourishing
sections.rationale: This issue tests the central inferential bridge from biological and human facts to action-guiding oughts, including whether flourishing clarifies the standard or expands it beyond survival without an objective warrant.

sections.title: Rational Egoism, Rights, and Moral Agency
sections.rationale: This issue addresses whether a life-centered ethic can derive interpersonal rights and constraints on advantageous harm, and whether psychopath and abnormal-agent cases expose circularity or legitimate limits on moral concepts.

sections.title: Animals, Harm, and Practical Boundaries
sections.rationale: This issue examines whether the competing accounts consistently explain concern for suffering, condemnation of gratuitous harm, differences between human and animal status, and permissibility claims about animal use.

motionBridge.description: Show that objective values, duties, human significance, and accountability jointly require God.

centralBridges.description: Ground intrinsic human worth and objective goodness in God's nature while explaining why naturalistic capacities or evolutionary origins are insufficient.
Ground categorical moral obligations in divine commands and distinguish genuine duties from social conditioning, agreement, or convention.
Explain why enduring moral significance and ultimate accountability require consequences beyond extinction and temporal human affairs.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain how divine accountability reconciles moral obligation with prudential reasons and supports responsible moral agency.
Distinguish fallible moral knowledge from objective truth and preserve transcultural criticism of conduct and institutions.

routes.description: Establish that stance-independent moral reasons, objective duties, human significance, and responsibility can be explained within secular moral realism without a divine ground or eternal consequences.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if secular accounts supply objective moral standards and categorical reasons, explain responsible agency and moral criticism, and show that finite harms, benefits, relationships, and actions retain real significance without cosmic permanence.

motionBridge.description: Show that secular moral realism can adequately ground every objective moral domain placed in dispute without requiring God.

centralBridges.description: Explain objective morality through desire-independent categorical reasons, substantive harm-and-help standards, or basic moral facts.
Explain moral requirements through decisive reasons or fair rational agreement without presupposing a personal lawgiver.
Ground genuine human significance in the objective importance of finite lives, harms, relationships, and actions rather than eternal cosmic effects.
Ground responsibility in rational agency and defend the authority of moral reasons even when morality conflicts with prudential self-interest.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain disagreement and historical moral error as compatible with objective truth and corrigible through reflective reasoning.
Demonstrate how secular principles yield determinate judgments about atrocities, innocent victims, and harms to sentient animals.

sections.title: Objective Value and Intrinsic Human Worth
sections.rationale: The motion requires an account of what makes value stance-independent and whether human worth is grounded by God, rational capacities, harm, or irreducible moral facts.

sections.title: Moral Duty, Categorical Reasons, and Lawgiving
sections.rationale: The principal grounding clash concerns whether genuine obligation needs divine command or can arise from objective reasons, rational agreement, and mutual moral authority.

sections.title: Rational Agency and Naturalistic Grounding
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether reflective capacities can explain moral responsibility and wrongness, or merely identify valuable features whose objective status still requires a deeper ground.

sections.title: Finite Life, Extinction, and Moral Significance
sections.rationale: The competing routes must establish whether actions and relationships need eternal consequences to matter objectively or possess genuine importance within finite human lives.

sections.title: Accountability, Salvation, and Prudential Conflict
sections.rationale: The accountability burden includes ultimate justice, the relation between morality and self-interest, and whether the proposed theistic mechanism consistently delivers deserved consequences.

sections.title: Moral Knowledge, Progress, and Practical Application
sections.rationale: Disagreement, historical error, atrocities, and treatment of animals test whether each foundation supports reliable moral criticism and substantive guidance without conflating access with truth.

routes.description: Establish God as the required transcendent ground of change, contingency, natural order, and objective moral obligation, while defending natural theology as a legitimate inference from observable effects.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the relevant features of reality require an ultimate actual, necessary, intelligent, and moral source; that source is adequately connected to God; and the skeptical alternatives do not remove those explanatory requirements.

motionBridge.description: Connect the cumulative metaphysical, natural-order, and moral inferences to an entity sufficiently characterized as God.

centralBridges.description: Show that change, instrumental causation, or contingency cannot be fully explained without a first actual or necessary foundation.
Show that stable natural regularity or mind-independent intelligible order requires grounding in a directing intellect.
Show that objective moral obligations exist independently of human preference and require a divine intellectual source.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Defend inference from natural effects to an extranatural explanation as methodologically legitimate rather than an appeal to ignorance.
Account for hiddenness, evil, and the interpersonal character of religious knowledge consistently with the proposed divine source.

routes.description: Maintain that belief in God should be withheld unless the affirmative defines and demonstrates a divine being, and show that the offered metaphysical, scientific, moral, and experiential considerations do not meet that burden.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the affirmative inferences remain unsupported, admit nondivine or secular alternatives, or fail to establish the attributes needed for God, making provisional nonbelief the warranted motion-level conclusion.

motionBridge.description: Show that no presented line supplies adequate evidence or a sound inference establishing a sufficiently defined God.

centralBridges.description: Challenge the move from observed change or causation to a timeless first source and from any such source to a divine mind.
Require independent grounds for supernatural explanations and preserve acknowledged ignorance where natural evidence is incomplete.
Show that moral judgment and objective assessment can operate through stated standards, facts, and shared interests without divine grounding.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Require an assessable definition of God and evidence connecting any inferred explanation to the claimed classical divine attributes.
Test private revelation, religious experience, and divine hiddenness against public demonstrability and alternative explanations.

sections.title: Burden of Proof, Definition, and Rational Nonbelief
sections.rationale: This issue fixes what each side must establish, whether atheism is merely withheld belief or a broader position, and how clearly the proposed God must be defined before the existence claim can be accepted.

sections.title: Thomistic Change, Causation, and Necessary Foundation
sections.rationale: The first-mover, causal-regress, and contingency arguments form the principal metaphysical route from ordinary dependent reality to a transcendent foundation, including the disputed transition from that foundation to God.

sections.title: Natural Order and the Method of Extranatural Inference
sections.rationale: This section addresses whether natural regularity, explanatory principles, universals, and cosmological models license inference to an intelligent or extranatural source, and what evidential constraints govern such an inference.

sections.title: Objective Morality and Divine Grounding
sections.rationale: The moral-law dispute is an independent major route to God and turns on the existence and meaning of moral objectivity, the adequacy of secular standards, and whether obligation or altruism indicates a divine intellect.

sections.title: Divine Hiddenness, Religious Knowledge, and Evil
sections.rationale: These issues test whether the proposed God is compatible with persistent nonbelief and suffering, and whether interpersonal or experiential knowledge can provide warranted support beyond publicly demonstrable evidence.

routes.description: Establish that evolutionary naturalism supplies defeaters for rational confidence in the cognitive faculties used to affirm naturalism, without requiring proof that a supernatural alternative is true.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if naturalism's account of belief formation leaves no adequate warrant for trusting human cognition about ultimate reality and the objection cannot be answered merely by demanding evidence of the supernatural.

motionBridge.description: Show that a worldview which undermines warrant for the cognition affirming it cannot itself be rationally affirmed.

centralBridges.description: Establish that physical determination, randomness, or causally idle mental states do not by themselves make beliefs responsive to rational grounds or truth.
Establish that selection for survival and reproduction does not ensure reliable cognition when faculties are extended to comprehensive metaphysical conclusions.
Establish that naturalism may be rejected or rational confidence withheld because of internal incoherence without first demonstrating a supernatural realm.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Distinguish metaphysical naturalism from scientific method and require a positive defense of the claim that only nature exists.
Test whether naturalism permits any contrary observation to count against it rather than automatically receiving a natural reinterpretation.

routes.description: Defend rational confidence in naturalism through provisional reliance on cognition, evolved capacities for dependable interaction, and publicly testable evidence while assigning the supernatural claimant the burden of demonstrating an addition to the known natural world.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if objective inquiry supplies a workable basis for corrigible confidence in natural conclusions, the evolutionary reliability objection does not establish global defeat, and no verified supernatural exception displaces the natural account.

motionBridge.description: Show that naturalism remains rationally warranted by objective evidence unless its alleged self-defeat is established or a supernatural exception is demonstrated.

centralBridges.description: Account for sufficiently dependable cognition through unavoidable provisional reliance on experience, evolved social capacities, and correction by shared objective inquiry.
Challenge the asserted connections among naturalism, determinism, survival-directed evolution, and the conclusion that rational thought is unwarranted.
Require independent, repeatable, objective verification before adding supernatural entities or causes to the accepted natural world.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Distinguish evidence-governed methodological naturalism and acceptance of the known physical world from an unsupported universal negative about every immaterial possibility.
Specify observable conditions that could support supernatural claims and use repeated testing to preserve revisability rather than immunity from contrary evidence.

sections.title: Naturalism's Definition and Burden of Proof
sections.rationale: The dispute over whether naturalism asserts that only nature exists or provisionally accepts the known natural world determines what each side must establish and whether internal critique can resolve the motion.

sections.title: Physical Causation, Determinism, and Rational Agency
sections.rationale: The claimed gap between physical belief production and responsiveness to reasons is a major proposed mechanism of self-defeat, while objections concerning indeterminism, emergence, and rational processes test that inference.

sections.title: Evolutionary Fitness and Truth-Tracking Cognition
sections.rationale: Whether selection for survival can produce faculties reliable enough for abstract worldview judgments is the principal substantive clash identified by the motion and the central evolutionary component of both routes.

sections.title: Objective Evidence, Experience, and Cognitive Correction
sections.rationale: Appeals to testable data, provisional sensory trust, social cooperation, and collaborative checking bear directly on whether naturalism can justify corrigible confidence despite acknowledged cognitive limitations.

sections.title: Falsifiability and Evidence Beyond Nature
sections.rationale: Competing standards for miracles, prophecy, apparent design, and other purported supernatural effects test both naturalism's openness to disconfirmation and whether any alternative has met the proposed evidential threshold.

routes.description: Establish a personal transcendent creator through the universe's beginning, connect objective morality to a good divine foundation, and use the resurrection case to identify the creator with Christian theism, while showing that observed suffering and the evil-God analogy do not defeat that cumulative case.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if its origin, moral, and resurrection components jointly support the Christian God and if the evidential inference from suffering is undercut by morally sufficient reasons or limits on human probability judgments without leaving the evil-God hypothesis evidentially symmetrical.

motionBridge.description: The cumulative arguments must support the existence of the Christian God strongly enough to withstand both the evidential problem of suffering and the evil-God symmetry challenge.

centralBridges.description: The universe's beginning must warrant a transcendent, immaterial, timeless, powerful, personal cause rather than mere unexplained origin.
Objective moral values and duties must require a divine foundation capable of supplying the creator's good moral character.
The historical resurrection case must discriminate in favor of divine action and connect generic creator reasoning to specifically Christian theism.
Apparently gratuitous suffering and the mirrored evil-God hypothesis must not warrant rejection of a good God once the full cumulative case and possible divine purposes are considered.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Human cognitive and historical limitations must materially constrain judgments that particular suffering lacks a morally sufficient providential purpose.
Divine goodness must rest on grounds other than a simple inductive inventory of worldly goods if the observational mirror is to misdescribe the theistic inference.

routes.description: Use the scale of apparently gratuitous suffering to disconfirm an omnipotent good God, show that standard defenses and appeals to inscrutable purposes transfer to an evil creator, and contest whether the cosmological, moral, and resurrection arguments supply the asymmetry or cumulative support required for Christian theism.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if suffering remains substantial evidence against the good-God hypothesis, Craig's defenses fail to distinguish it from the parallel evil-God hypothesis, and the affirmative arguments do not independently establish the creator's goodness or specifically Christian identity strongly enough to overcome that challenge.

motionBridge.description: Observed suffering and evil-God symmetry must prevent Craig's cumulative arguments from establishing the good Christian God specified by the motion.

centralBridges.description: The quantity, intensity, and history of sentient suffering must provide evidential grounds for excluding an omnipotent and perfectly good deity.
Free will, stable laws, soul-making, compensation, and unknown-purpose defenses must be shown to transfer materially from a good God to an evil creator.
The moral argument must fail to establish a divine foundation for objective morality capable of breaking the good-God and evil-God symmetry.
The cosmological and resurrection arguments must fail to identify a good Christian God or to outweigh the observational evidence invoked against that hypothesis.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Rational exclusion of a specified deity must remain possible even without a complete alternative explanation of cosmic origins or suffering.
The evidential challenge must be formulable through excessive suffering without presupposing objective evil or the moral realism disputed by the moral argument.

sections.title: Cosmological Cause and the Creator's Moral Character
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether the universe's beginning establishes a personal transcendent creator and whether that conclusion contributes anything toward choosing between a good creator, an evil creator, and a morally unspecified cause.

sections.title: Objective Morality and Its Proposed Divine Foundation
sections.rationale: The moral argument is the principal bridge from a morally neutral creator to divine goodness, while its premises, atheist-compatible alternatives, and relationship to suffering determine whether it can break the central symmetry.

sections.title: Resurrection Evidence and Christian Identification
sections.rationale: The resurrection argument supplies the specifically Christian component of the cumulative case, making the reliability and discriminatory force of extraordinary historical testimony necessary issues rather than merely generic evidence for a creator.

sections.title: Suffering, Feasible Worlds, and Morally Sufficient Reasons
sections.rationale: The scale of sentient suffering is the principal observational evidence against a perfectly good God, and the dispute over feasible alternatives, providential purposes, and human epistemic limits directly governs that inference.

sections.title: Evil-God Symmetry and Observational Inference
sections.rationale: The defining comparative challenge asks whether defenses of a good God can be mirrored for an evil creator and whether observation may exclude a morally specified deity without serving as a positive argument for its opposite.

routes.description: Establish that the existence of severe natural and moral evil does not make belief in an omnipotent, perfectly good God unreasonable when logical compatibility, human epistemic limits, theistic purposes, and the wider evidential context are considered together.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if it supplies a coherent basis for God and evil to coexist, blocks the inference from apparently gratuitous suffering to divine improbability, and explains why the full evidential and doctrinal context can preserve rational theistic belief.

motionBridge.description: Connect the answers to logical and evidential evil with the conclusion that theistic belief remains reasonable on the total evidence.

centralBridges.description: Show that omnipotence and perfect goodness do not logically contradict evil when significant freedom or morally sufficient permission is possible.
Show that limited human knowledge of causal consequences and providential purposes undercuts confident judgments that suffering is gratuitous.
Show how knowledge of God, freely accepted salvation, eternal life, or other divine purposes can alter the expected significance of earthly suffering.
Require the probability of God to be assessed against the whole body of relevant evidence rather than the existence of evil in isolation.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain how judgments that suffering is objectively evil may contribute to an affirmative moral case for a transcendent foundation.
Account for how complex contingencies could serve divine purposes while preserving meaningful creaturely freedom.

routes.description: Establish that the scale and character of suffering make belief in an almighty, all-loving, and humanly concerned deity unreasonable because proposed appeals to freedom, unknown goods, salvation, or wider evidence do not reconcile those attributes with the actual world.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if observed suffering provides a warranted adverse inference about divine goodness or power, the principal theistic defenses fail to explain a feasible better world or justify extreme harms, and secular accounts preserve moral judgment without God.

motionBridge.description: Connect the cumulative force of natural and moral suffering with the conclusion that belief in the relevant deity is unreasonable.

centralBridges.description: Show why tsunamis, childhood cancer, and comparable harms conflict evidentially with combined omnipotence, benevolence, and concern for conscious creatures.
Require an explanation of why an omnipotent God could not create significantly free creatures in a world containing substantially less natural and moral evil.
Defend ordinary moral knowledge as adequate to judge extreme suffering despite uncertainty about remote causal consequences or alleged unknown goods.
Test whether appeals to inability, permissive greater goods, salvation, and mystery jointly preserve a coherent account of divine power and goodness.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Ground moral obligations and humane concern in facts about sentience, needs, suffering, sympathy, and shared human experience without invoking God.
Address how religious diversity and exclusivist salvation claims affect proposed salvific explanations of indiscriminate suffering.

sections.title: Logical Compatibility, Freedom, and Better Possible Worlds
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether God and evil are logically consistent and whether significant freedom or divine feasibility can explain why a world with substantially less evil was not actualized.

sections.title: Evidential Evil, Unknown Reasons, and Human Moral Knowledge
sections.rationale: This central clash determines whether apparently gratuitous suffering supports an adverse probability judgment or whether limited knowledge of consequences and divine reasons defeats that inference.

sections.title: Divine Purposes, Salvation, and Eternal Recompense
sections.rationale: This issue examines whether knowledge of God, salvation, providential purposes, and an afterlife make earthly suffering less surprising, and whether those claims adequately address severe and indiscriminate harms.

sections.title: Divine Attributes, the Actual World, and Total Evidence
sections.rationale: This section connects the character of the observed world and the wider evidential context to the motion-level question of whether belief in an omnipotent, loving, and concerned deity is reasonable.

sections.title: Objective Morality and the Foundation of Judgments About Evil
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether calling suffering objectively evil supports a transcendent moral foundation or whether natural facts about sentience, needs, and harm can ground moral obligations independently.

routes.description: Establish that objective moral values and duties require a transcendent personal ground, identify God's nature and authority as that ground, and show why evolutionary or material descriptions cannot supply binding normativity.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if it connects moral objectivity, obligation, and purpose to an invariant personal source while answering the principal naturalistic, arbitrariness, and moral-knowledge alternatives.

motionBridge.description: Show that God, understood as the personal ground of goodness and obligation, explains objective morality more completely than science, evolution, and human flourishing alone.

centralBridges.description: Establish that objective moral comparison, binding duties, and human purpose require a standard, authority, and telos beyond individual or social opinion.
Explain why empirical and evolutionary accounts of behavior do not by themselves generate prescriptive duties or an objective hierarchy among competing moral dispositions.
Defend God's nature as the nonarbitrary moral standard rather than locating goodness outside God or in contingent commands.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Connect trustworthy reasoning, freedom, and moral agency to a conception of persons not exhausted by blind material processes.
Distinguish questions about knowing or interpreting moral truths from the ontological question of what makes those truths objective.

routes.description: Establish an objective moral framework centered on sentient interests, autonomy, liberty, and flourishing; explain its evolutionary and empirical basis; and challenge the necessity and reliability of divine grounding.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if evolved moral capacities and reasoned attention to individual welfare support objective moral judgment while divine-command, scriptural, and theistic accounts face unresolved explanatory or epistemic objections.

motionBridge.description: Show that science, evolution, and principles of sentient flourishing can explain objective moral capacities and judgments without requiring a supernatural personal ground.

centralBridges.description: Account for empathy, fairness, reciprocity, and cooperation as evolved capacities that make moral understanding and social life possible.
Specify survival, flourishing, autonomy, liberty, and equal consideration as standards for judging conduct and constraining aggregate welfare.
Show why rival revelations, interpretive disagreement, historical revision, or contingent commands impede a reliable divine or scriptural moral method.

sections.title: The Ground of Objective Standards and Duties
sections.rationale: This section addresses the motion's primary ontological burden: whether objective moral standards and binding obligations require a personal divine source or can exist within a naturalistic account.

sections.title: Evolution, Flourishing, and the Is–Ought Bridge
sections.rationale: This section tests whether evolved capacities, cooperation, sentient welfare, autonomy, and flourishing can support prescriptive moral judgments rather than merely describe behavior and survival.

sections.title: Divine Authority, Revelation, and Moral Knowledge
sections.rationale: This section covers the relationship between moral grounding and moral access, including divine-command arbitrariness, scriptural interpretation, religious diversity, and the distinction between ontology and epistemology.

sections.title: Reason, Agency, and the Nature of Persons
sections.rationale: This section examines whether material and evolutionary processes can sustain trustworthy reasoning and responsible moral agency, or whether those capacities require an immaterial or theistic basis.

sections.title: Moral Progress, Rights, and Difficult Applications
sections.rationale: This section tests each framework through historical reform and contested cases involving equal rights, liberty, suffering, and conflicts between individual autonomy and collective welfare.

routes.description: Establish that the canonical Gospels are best connected to Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John through converging early attribution, text-specific internal features, and historically plausible forms of source use or authorized collaboration.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the attribution tradition and internal indicators jointly identify the traditional figures or their authority more plausibly than a later naming process, while accounting for anonymity, Greek literary composition, source dependence, and oral transmission.

motionBridge.description: Connect each canonical Gospel to its traditional namesake as writer, source, or authorizing authority in the sense required by the motion.

centralBridges.description: Show that the timing, distribution, consistency, and content of early testimony preserve genuine authorship information rather than a dependent later convention.
Show that salient textual features independently fit the proposed Matthean, Petrine-Markan, Lukan, and Johannine connections.
Show that differences in education and language are compatible with traditional authority through source use, assistants, or collaborative literary production.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain why formally unnamed narratives or third-person narration do not sever an otherwise supported connection to traditional authors.
Explain how oral circulation, literary dependence, and selective narration can remain closely grounded in apostolic testimony.

routes.description: Establish that the canonical texts do not supply adequate identifications of Matthew, Mark, Luke, or John and that their literary characteristics and attribution history are better explained by anonymous educated authors and later church naming.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the evidence fails to connect the canonical texts to the traditional figures or their authorization, while anonymous circulation, educational mismatch, and the emergence and propagation of later names provide a coherent alternative account.

motionBridge.description: Show that neither direct composition nor authorization by the four traditional figures is adequately established for the canonical Gospels.

centralBridges.description: Show that securely identifiable traditional names arise too late or dependently to establish knowledge of original authorship.
Show that the language, education, and compositional demands of the texts conflict with authorship by the traditional Galilean disciples.
Show that first-person passages, eyewitness claims, narrative details, and conventional author labels do not identify the traditional figures.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Provide a historically coherent reason authoritative communities could assign and then preserve apostolically useful names.
Distinguish attested dictation or letter-writing assistance from independent composition of lengthy literary narratives for an illiterate authority.

sections.title: Timing, independence, and reach of external attribution

sections.rationale: The motion turns partly on whether the traditional figures could compose the Greek narratives themselves or exercise authorship authority through assistants, sources, and collaborative production.

sections.rationale: Travel narration, eyewitness claims, disciple rosters, Petrine features, and Matthean characteristics matter insofar as they identify particular authors rather than merely remaining compatible with them.

sections.title: Source dependence, oral transmission, and apostolic proximity
